newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian chief asked Kohl to intervene with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Colombian chief asked Kohl to intervene with U.S..

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper asked German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to help ease the crisis in U.S.-Colombian ties last summer, when Washington revoked his U.S. travel visa because of his alleged ties to drug lords, a leading newspaper reported on Monday.

In a letter to Kohl dated July 11, the day on which the United States took the extraordinary step of revoking his visa, Samper also asked for Kohl's help in restarting peace talks with leftist guerrillas and in cracking down on Colombia's powerful drug cartels.

A copy of the letter was published in Monday's editions of El Tiempo, Colombia's most influential daily. Spokesmen for Samper and for the German Embassy in Bogota said they were unable to confirm or deny its authenticity.

In the letter, El Tiempo said, Samper lamented the "great tension" in Colombia's relations with Washington. He did not refer directly to having had his visa revoked by Washington on the official grounds that he had "pursued policies designed to protect and further the interests of the drug cartels."

U.S.-Colombia ties had already plunged to their lowest point since Washington engineered Panama's secession from Colombia at the turn of the century. The United States removed Colombia in March from a list of countries deemed fully cooperative in fighting the drug trade, citing among other reasons charges that Samper's 1994 election campaign was partly financed by Cali cartel drug traffickers.

In June, when the lower house of Colombia's Congress voted to clear Samper of any wrongdoing, Washington escalated threats to impose economic sanctions on Bogota. And it was outraged in late June when Colombia rejected a U.S. request for the extradition of four drug kingpins.

"We're very interested in dissipating the tension and in reestablishing a relationship of trust and cooperation with the North Americans that will allow us to advance, increasingly, in the fight against drug trafficking and all the other problems affecting our society," the letter said.

"We also believe that in this regard the mediation of the chancellor of the German government could be definitive," it reportedly added. "We are certain that with your collaboration, which we thank you for in advance, we will achieve solutions in a very short time frame that will be well received by the international community."

The letter appealed to Kohl and Bernd Schmidbauer, the coordinator of Bonn's intelligence services, for help in arranging peace talks with leftist rebels. And it asked for the German government's "collaboration, observations and suggestions" about ways of intensifying Colombia's fight against the drug trade.

Publication of the letter comes amidst a mushrooming Colombian political scandal over the arrest of shadowy German private agent Werner Mauss, who is being held along with his wife on suspicion of involvement in a Colombian kidnap case and deals with National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrillas.

Opposition lawmakers have called for the resignation or dismissal of Interior Minister Horacio Serpa because he has acknowledged that he held talks with Mauss and stayed at his residence during an official visit to Germany in mid-July.
